title: CPiRi: Channel Permutation-Invariant Relational Interaction for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
one_liner: A forecasting model that learns to predict multiple measurement channels together, but stays accurate even when those channels are shuffled or new ones arrive.
lead: When you track multiple quantities at once (like temperature and humidity in a building), current forecasting models either memorize which channel is which (and break when channels swap) or treat them independently (and miss how they connect). CPiRi learns to find the real relationships between channels from the data itself, so it works even when channels are reordered or new ones are added.

paras: In multivariate forecasting (predicting multiple measurement channels at once), there are two kinds of models. The first kind learns how the channels depend on each other — if temperature drops, maybe humidity drops too — but it memorizes which channel is in which slot. The second kind treats each channel completely separately to stay flexible, but then it never learns that humidity and temperature are connected.

The trap: the first model breaks if you rearrange which channel is first, which is second. The second model misses the relationships entirely and makes worse predictions. A real system needs both: learn the actual dependencies, but not care about which slot a channel sits in.

callout.b: The central problem in one sentence.
callout.html: Current models either memorize channel positions and break when channels move, or treat channels separately and miss how they connect.

panels.title: 1. The old way: channel order matters
panels.caption: Model learns: first channel always leads; second follows. Order is hardcoded.

panels.title: 2. Shuffle the channels: everything breaks
panels.caption: Same channels, different slots. Model is now confused and predicts wrong.

panels.title: 3. CPiRi learns relationships, not positions
panels.caption: Model asks: which channels actually influence which, regardless of slot?

panels.title: 4. Shuffling does not break the learned relationships
panels.caption: Channels rearranged; learned dependencies still hold. Predictions stay accurate.

panels.title: 5. Even new channels work because relationships are slot-free
panels.caption: Add a sixth channel; model finds how it fits into the learned dependency web.

steps.text: A frozen pretrained encoder pulls out what is changing in time within each channel.
A lightweight module learns which channels truly influence each other, using the temporal features as evidence.
Each training batch rearranges channel positions to force the model to ignore slot and rely on learned structure.
The model uses the learned relationships plus the temporal features to make a forecast.
Once trained, the model works with channels in any order or with new channels, because relationships are not tied to positions.

paras: The paper changes how the model learns which channels influence each other. Instead of baking channel positions into the learned weights (so position 1 always talks to position 2), it learns the structure as a flexible pattern that holds regardless of which slot each channel occupies.

hidden.name: inter-channel influence structure
paras: The hidden quantity is which channels actually depend on each other — the real dependency web between measurements, independent of their slot numbers. For example, in a building, humidity might influence temperature, and both might influence pressure, but this structure exists regardless of whether humidity is stored in column 1 or column 5.

CPiRi estimates this by training on shuffled versions of the same data. When the model sees the same channels in different orders and is forced to make the same predictions, it must learn the true structure, not the slot-position mapping. The channels that consistently influence a target are marked as important; those that do not are marked as unimportant.

heat.caption: Darker: stronger influence. Highlighted: the most reliable relationships learned from data.

reads.html: The model learns a map of which measurements influence which, then uses that map to predict, ignoring which column each measurement sits in.
The paper uses permutation-invariant regularization: shuffling channel order during training forces the model to learn relationships that generalize across all permutations.

paras: The core mechanism: if you train a model on the same data but with channels shuffled in each batch, the model must learn patterns that hold regardless of slot order. A weight that says 'always trust slot 1' fails when slot 1 changes. But a weight that says 'temperature correlates with humidity' succeeds no matter which column holds temperature.

CPiRi works in two layers. First, a frozen temporal encoder extracts signals from each channel independently — it captures what is changing in time. Second, a lightweight spatial module learns which temporal signals matter for predicting which other signals, using only the content of the signals, never their positions. By shuffling channels during training, the spatial module is forced to infer 'temperature and humidity are related' rather than 'slot 1 and slot 2 are related.' Once trained, this structure is portable: it works with channels in any order or with new channels, because the learned dependencies are slot-free.

stages.s: frozen temporal encoder extracts what is changing in each channel
spatial module learns which channels influence which (slot-free)
shuffle training data to reinforce slot-free learning
stable predictions under any channel order

math.words: Total loss is the forecast error plus a penalty that pushes the learned structure to stay the same when channels are shuffled.
symbols: squared error between predicted and true next values
learned channel relationship structure from input X
same input X but with channel columns shuffled
the distance between two structures (how different they are)
how strongly to enforce that relationships stay consistent across shuffles

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we train on temperature and humidity. In batch 1, columns are [temp, humidity]. The spatial module learns that temp leads humidity (relationship R1). In batch 2, columns are [humidity, temp]. The module learns that temp still leads humidity (relationship R2). The penalty term ||R1 - R2|| is near zero — the learned structure is the same either way.

If a naive model tried to memorize 'column 1 always leads', R1 and R2 would be opposite, and the penalty would be large, forcing retraining. With CPiRi, the penalty stays low because the model learned the true structure, not the slot mapping.
Over many shuffled batches, the model converges to a single, slot-free structure that minimizes both prediction error and shuffling penalties.

math.note: The permutation-invariant penalty ensures the model learns which channels truly depend on each other, not which slot is which.

charts.title: Standard channel-dependent model
charts.note: Model memorizes channel positions; loses accuracy when order changes or new channels arrive.

charts.title: CPiRi model
charts.note: Model learns slot-free relationships; stays accurate across shuffles and generalizes to new channels.

items.html: If the temporal patterns in a dataset are very different from the pretrained encoder's training data, the encoder might not extract useful features, forcing the spatial module to work with weak signals. This limits the model's ability to adapt to time series with unfamiliar patterns.

items.b: Channel relationships are learned, not guaranteed to match real causal structure.
items.html: The model learns statistical associations (correlation), not true causation. If two channels correlate by coincidence or due to a hidden third factor, the model might learn a misleading relationship, leading to poor predictions when the coincidence breaks.

items.b: Shuffling penalty can be too weak or too strong.
items.html: If lambda is too small, permutation invariance is not enforced strongly enough and the model drifts back to memorizing positions. If lambda is too large, the model overshoots and fails to capture legitimate channel differences, hurting accuracy on the original order.

items.b: Done right: cross-validate lambda and test the model on shuffled and new-channel versions of a held-out test set.
items.html: Choose lambda by measuring how much shuffling degrades accuracy; aim for minimal loss of accuracy when channels are reordered. Validate on held-out data with both shuffled orders and new channels added, to confirm the model truly learned slot-free relationships.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy multivariate time series: generate 4 or 5 channels (for example, sine waves with different frequencies and phase offsets to simulate temperature, humidity, pressure). Train CPiRi on the dataset. Then, in three separate tests: (1) Predict on the original channel order and measure accuracy. (2) Shuffle the channels randomly and predict again, measuring accuracy. (3) Add one new channel (a sine wave not seen during training) and predict, measuring accuracy. The demo passes if all three accuracies are within 2-3 percentage points of each other, showing that the model learned a slot-free, generalizable structure.
demo.metric_eq: stability score = min(acc_original, acc_shuffled, acc_new_channel) / max(acc_original, acc_shuffled, acc_new_channel)
demo.closing: If the ratio is above 0.95, the model is truly permutation-invariant and generalizes to new channels. If it is below 0.90, the model has regressed to memorizing positions.
